content: Tenapanor is indicated for the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) in adults. The recommended dosage is 50 mg taken orally twice daily, immediately before breakfast and dinner. Tenapanor is also indicated as an add-on therapy to reduce serum phosphorus levels in adults with chronic kidney disease (CKD) on dialysis. This is specifically for patients who have an inadequate response to phosphate binders or are intolerant to any dose of phosphate binder therapy. The recommended dosage for this indication is 30 mg taken orally twice daily, immediately before breakfast and dinner. Serum phosphorus levels should be monitored, and the dosage adjusted as needed to manage gastrointestinal tolerability. No dose adjustments are required for patients with renal or hepatic impairment. The safety and efficacy of tenapanor have not been established in patients under 18 years of age. It is contraindicated in children under 6 years of age due to the risk of severe dehydration, as observed in studies with young juvenile rats. Use in children aged 6 to less than 12 years should be avoided for the same reason. Tenapanor is minimally absorbed systemically, with plasma concentrations below the limit of quantification. Maternal use is not expected to result in fetal drug exposure. There is no available data on the presence of tenapanor in human or animal milk, its effects on milk production, or its effects on breastfed infants. However, the minimal systemic absorption of tenapanor is not expected to result in clinically relevant exposure to breastfed infants. Tenapanor inhibits the intestinal uptake transporter OATP2B1, which may reduce the exposure of OATP2B1 substrates. This interaction has been observed with several drugs, including atorvastatin, bosentan, conjugated estrogens, enalapril, fexofenadine, fluvastatin, glyburide, pravastatin, and rosuvastatin. For these drugs, caution should be exercised, and monitoring is recommended. In the case of enalapril, the peak exposure (Cmax) of enalapril and its active metabolite, enalaprilat, decreases significantly when co-administered with tenapanor. Blood pressure should be monitored, and the dosage of enalapril increased if needed. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate can decrease the level or effect of tenapanor by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Therapy should be modified, and administration should be separated by at least three hours. Close monitoring is advised. Diarrhea may occur as a side effect of tenapanor. If severe diarrhea develops, dosing should be suspended, and the patient should be rehydrated. Tenapanor should be stored at 68–77°F (20–25°C), with excursions permitted to 59–86°F (15–30°C). It should be kept in its tightly closed original container, protected from moisture. The desiccant should not be removed from the bottle, and the medication should not be subdivided or repackaged. For pregnant women, tenapanor is generally considered acceptable, as controlled studies have shown no evidence of fetal risk. Tenapanor is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4/5, and low levels of its major metabolite, M1, are detected in plasma. Approximately 70% of the drug is excreted in feces and 9% in urine. Patients should take tenapanor immediately before breakfast or the first meal of the day and immediately before dinner.
